title: The cypress tree
hook: asked why Bodhidharma came, Zhaozhou answers: the cypress tree in the garden (Gateless Gate 37)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a monk asked what Buddha is, and Dongshan said three pounds of flax. Your line: three pounds of flax. What did you lift, and did you feel its weight before the thoughts came? Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

Three days ago, a man hung from a tree by his teeth while someone below asked why Bodhidharma came from the west. Today the same question comes back, and this time it gets an answer. A monk puts it to Zhaozhou, an old Chan teacher: why did Bodhidharma come from the west? What is the heart of all this? Zhaozhou doesn't lecture. He doesn't open a book. He points the monk, as it were, out the window. The cypress tree in front of the garden. Case thirty-seven of the Gateless Gate is that short. Today, the tree.
screen: `THE QUESTION COMES BACK.` → `ZHAOZHOU DOESN'T LECTURE.` → `THE CYPRESS TREE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Bodhidharma is the teacher tradition says carried the Chan way from India to China. Asking why he came is a way of asking what the whole tradition is for. It's the same question the man in the tree was asked, and here a teacher actually answers it. Second, the answer. Zhaozhou names a tree, in a courtyard, right there. Not a symbol, not a parable. A tree you could walk over and touch. Like yesterday's flax, it refuses to send the monk off somewhere else for the meaning. The answer to the big question is standing in the yard. Third, a detail for the curious. The Chinese word in the case names a cypress or juniper kind of tree. Some English versions of the Gateless Gate call it an oak. So depending on which book you pick up, Zhaozhou is pointing at a different tree. The koan doesn't seem to mind. Whatever is in front of you is the point. Fourth, why it lands. Some questions in a life seem to need a faraway answer: a different job, a different city, a different self. Zhaozhou's reply turns the head around. The tree was there before the question and will be there after it. In koan practice, the point isn't an essay on trees. The student is asked to meet the tree, or whatever is in front of them, so fully that there's nothing left over to explain.
screen: `WHY DID BODHIDHARMA COME?` · `A TREE IN THE COURTYARD.` · `CYPRESS, JUNIPER, OR OAK.` · `IT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.` · then, large: `THE CYPRESS IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Find one tree: out a window, down the street, or in memory, a tree you know well. Look at it, or bring it to mind clearly. The bark. The way the branches split. Where the light hits it. Don't name its species or think about what it stands for. Just let it be a tree, in front of you, now. When the mind wanders off to the next thing, come back to the tree. Breathe with it for a while. The bell holds the time.
The cypress tree. Zhaozhou's answer when asked why Bodhidharma came from the west, case thirty-seven of the Gateless Gate: the tree in front of the garden. Today's word.
Your line: the cypress in the garden. Today, when a big question tugs at you, look up at one tree, or whatever is in front of you, for a full breath. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

screen: `DAY 1245 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TOP OF THE POLE.`

howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen training this case is given as a koan, and students carry the phrase 'the cypress tree in front of the garden' through sitting and work until they can present it to the teacher.

original.note: Chinese: 'the cypress tree in front of the garden'. 柏 names a cypress or juniper. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a symbol of something deep.
what it means: a real tree in a real courtyard, given as the whole answer.
what a scholar hears: 柏, a cypress or juniper, rendered 'oak' in some English versions; Gateless Gate case 37, from Zhaozhou.

notes: Case 37 paraphrased. Confirm the answer 庭前柏樹子 and that 柏 is a cypress/juniper-type tree.
'Some English versions call it an oak' refers to the Senzaki/Reps rendering ('the oak tree in the garden'); 'that version traveled widely' is a soft claim; cut if a Keeper prefers.
'Northern China' for Zhaozhou: his town lay in the north (Hebei); confirm or cut.
Bodhidharma bringing Chan from India attributed to tradition. 'A stock question in the old records' is stated without a count; confirm.
'Some questions in a life seem to they need a faraway answer' is about questions, not about a group of people; soften if needed.

Editor pass: fixed a garbled line ('seem to they need'); cut unsupported claims (northern China, 'stock question in the old records', 'traveled widely', the monk walking past the tree, what teachers want); screen and fork reveal adjusted to match.
